utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. Boris Zorko, Chad Mair, Deirdre Montgomery, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we would now call our next witness to the stand, Mr. Carl Bildt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, we see a second person coming in with Mr. Carl Bildt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we do. I will inquire as to who that second person is, because I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we start the proceedings today, could you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Carl Bildt is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I see that you have somebody with you in attendance in court. Could you please identify who that individual is for us?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mrs. Anette Brolenius.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could we understand in what capacity is Ms. Brolenius here?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: She is from the Embassy -- the Swedish Embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do I understand that you require her assistance during your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that satisfies the Chamber's inquiry with regard to the individual who is accompanying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Welcome to The Hague, Mr. Bildt.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I think we all appreciate, you are an individual who was intimately involved in bringing to a conclusion the conflict in the Balkans. But before we discuss those matters, if you would be so kind as to give us a rough, not necessarily terribly extensive, indication of your background.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the sense of a curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: In the sense of my curriculum vitae, I think that is fairly well known. I have been member of parliament in Sweden for -- in the order of quarter of a century, although that was quite some time ago. I was prime minister of my country. I was intensely involved in different international affairs. And what is perhaps of relevance for the Tribunal is the fact that I was then, from early June, I think, of 1995, appointed as the European Union co-chairman of the International Conference on Former Yugoslavia and served in that capacity until the dissolution of ICFY, which was a gradual process, but the de facto dissolution of ICFY, and continued then in different, other working capacities as High Representative in Sarajevo for two years and later as the Special Envoy of the Secretariat of the United Nations for the Balkans, But that brings us into the Kosovo war, so that is at a later stage of the dramas of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And with regard to -- with regard to the EU special representative position that you held, who did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I succeeded Lord Owen who served from the setting up of that institution, whenever that could have been, in 1993 or something like that. And he had served for that period and I succeeded him in early June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the Dayton peace talks, if I'm not mistaken, you were one of the two co-chairmen of the Dayton peace talks, were you not?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I was. Or three, to be precise. I think there were three -- formally speaking, there were three vice-chairman, or whatever it was called at the time, of the Dayton peace talks. It was Richard Holbrooke, who was assistant secretary of state for the United States at the time; there was myself for the European Union; and there was Mr. Igor Ivanov, who was the first deputy foreign minister of the Russian Federation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Above and beyond that service, it's my understanding that you're associated with a number of international organisations and serve on advisory boards for the centre for European Reform --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Did. As foreign minister of Sweden, I had no other responsibility but the responsibilities to my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the result of the recent election?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. That is the result of the Swedish Constitution. That's the way it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: If you are a foreign minister or member of the cabinet, that's what you are, nothing else. Then I have been quite a number of things in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: But that was in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the past you were -- served on that advisory board, the Centre for European Reform?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Among others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The Aspen Institute?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. But I certainly attended a lot of the -- well, the Aspen Institute Italia, yes, quite, the Italian branch. That's true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And RAND Europe?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Not RAND Europe. But I was on the board of trustees of RAND Corporation in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. I take it that you were then also a member of the council for international -- of the international institute of strategic studies in London?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You at one point in time, I believe, you had your own news letter. I don't know if you are still doing that?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, depends on how you define things. But I have always been fairly active on the Internet in different ways, newsletters or blogs or whatever. So you can find my digital track record is rather extensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you have published a number of works?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've published a number of works --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I published a number of works, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And including in that, you published the book "The Country that Stepped Out In The Cold" in 1972.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "A Future in Freedom" in 1976?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're a citizen of Holland, Sweden and --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Halland, not Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Halland, yes --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Halland is a province of Sweden. Holland is a country of the European Union and that's always a confusion, but anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's Halland with an A not with an O.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Halland.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Holland is a different place.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "The Only Way" in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I saw the note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The court reporter asks that you guys slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "The Only Way" in 1994?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally, from -- for our purposes, a book which I think is pertinent to our considerations, "Peace Journey."

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: 1997 in the Swedish edition and then the English version that we referred to in 1998. Later in versions in the local languages but that is perhaps not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us what honours or decorations you have been awarded?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I can't. If you had asked me I could have brought a list. But I can supply that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. They do include, as I understand it, from the France the commander of the Legion of Honour?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I think that is the -- I'm somewhat uncertain about the rank, but, yes. I can certainly supply all of this for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. From Germany?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Estonia?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Latvia?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I'm not mistaken, you are also a member or were a member of an organisation which I believe is called the Madrid Club?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, yeah, you can define that in different ways. Madrid Club is an informal organisation of former prime ministers. I am a former prime minister, but since I'm also serving cabinet member, I'm no longer part of that. There are several informal organisations of former prime ministers. I think there are three or four of them existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And your present duties are?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Foreign minister of Sweden, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to go back now to 1995. And I noticed that you have with you a number of documents. I take it there are things that you have with you that you may need to refer to in order to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to start in July of 1995. And I'd like to focus on July 7th, if I could. And ask you if you recall where you were on the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I don't immediately but since I got my book here, we can easily find it out. I had obviously been in Sarajevo on the 6th, and I arrived in Belgrade the day after, Friday, the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Belgrade on the 7th of July, who did you intend on meeting with at that time?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I intended to meet with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from President Milosevic, was it your intent at that time to meet with any other individuals?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. I met with diplomatic representatives in Belgrade. But from the -- what was called the Yugoslav side at the time still, I think, my intention was to meet with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall where you met with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. But I can find it out. It was in Dobanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you met --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: It was his -- as you know, his -- one of the Tito places --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: -- that he often frequented just outside Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in your meeting on July 7th with President Milosevic, do you recall who else was in attendance at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: From his side?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: From his side.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, during the part -- the first part of that meeting it was always the same. It was only his assistant by the name of Goran. You would know the name, I would assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- with regard to, just for the moment, the subsequent meetings that you had with President Milosevic in the month of July, would it be fair to say that this particular individual who you have identified as Goran was present at all meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I would say that there was apart from General Mladic, we might come to that, no one else present at those meetings. I would not necessarily say that this individual was present during every part of every meeting. But I can say that there was no one else from the -- let's call it Belgrade side that ever attended meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just so we're perfectly clear, when you say there was no one else who was present from the Belgrade side at those meetings, I'd like you to take a look to the back of the room and see whether you recognise General Perisic or not?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I -- I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was General Perisic at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. And I had no -- no contact with General Perisic whatsoever, nor any knowledge of his activities during the entire course of the Bosnian war. I had one meeting with General Perisic in -- after he had left the VJ and set up a political party, I can't really remember the name of it, in -- after the fall of Milosevic when I was in Belgrade and met with the different political representative, I met with him when he was chairman of his political party. That was the beginning of 2000, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: But we had no contact whatsoever and I really have no knowledge, either direct or indirect, about anything concerning him during the period of the Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned General Mladic. Did you have occasion to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you meet him on the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes. One of the occasions, yes. Late in the evening of the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recall how that came about, did you request to meet with General Mladic or --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: We did --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- did he request to meet with you?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. We did request. That was due to the overall situation at the time. As I think you are aware, I was responsible for essentially the political negotiations to get a settlement under what was called the Plan B after the de facto collapse of the Plan A, which was the contact group efforts in the preceding summer. At the same time -- at the same time as we were doing these political talks, which was my responsibility, the situation on the ground had deteriorated quite considerably and one of the effects of that was that the normal contacts that had been established or had been there between UNPROFOR, the UN forces, either UNPROFOR in Zagreb or BiH command in Sarajevo, and the Bosnian Serb forces, the VRS, had ceased. That was after the Pale bombing sometimes in May. That had led to the fact that there had not been any regular communications on quite a number of the different issues where there was a need, according to the UN command, to communicate, and I was asked to try to facilitate contact with General Mladic -- or we asked President Milosevic, to be quite frank, to facilitate a contact with General Mladic to see if there was any possibility of re-establishing contacts between the UN forces and the VRS in order to handle a number of different issues, notably the resupply issue to the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. You mentioned in your response Plan B. If you could, in a brief form explain to the Chamber what Plan B was.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite certain but I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Plan A was essentially the contact group effort of -- well, might go even further and say that the original attempt to settle the Bosnian war after the outbreak of the war. There had been attempts prior to the outbreak of the war in April of 1992 was it -- with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: That collapsed in 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was the Vance-Owen Plan the Plan A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, quite. Vance Owen. Then the -- what we refer -- what I refer to as Plan A was the contact group plan in the summer of 1994. Correct me if I -- 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Which had been the -- which was the product of rather extensive -- the contact group had then been established by the way, hadn't existed up to that time. It was established, and the contact group had major difficulties getting agreement on a plan to submit to the parties on the sort of take it or leave it basis. That was done sometime in July of that year, if I remember it. It consisted -- and I have a fairly extensive description of it in the book. It consisted primarily of a map, but the contact group had not been able to agree on the constitutional provisions. It was a take it or leave it. The contact group said you either take it or leave it, and in case you leave it, we're not going have any contacts with you. Now this was accepted sort of by Sarajevo. It was rejected sort of by Pale. I said rejected because Pale said, We want to see the constitutional provisions. So since there weren't any constitutional provisions, this was interpreted as a rejection, which it was, formally speaking. That meant that, of course, in accordance to what the contact group had said, contact ceased. The idea was then to go on the basis of that for direct negotiations between the parties. The parties I can describe as Sarajevo and Pale, for the sake of simplicity. That had then collapsed and the Sarajevo position, President Izetbegovic, to use a name, but not necessarily only him, was that accordingly there could be no contacts with Pale, with the Bosnian Serb leadership. Then after some considerable deliberations, I think, in the beginning of 1995, I think it was in March, the contact group reached agreement on what I refer to as Plan B. The Plan B was to go primarily to President Milosevic and say, Try to get agreement on a couple of different things. One was a recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign country. Number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Number two was an agreement on the basic outlines of constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, two entities, whatever they were to be called. That was a separate issue in itself, as well as the principle of division of the territory according to the 49, 51. And I think the third element, if I remember rightly, of that plan was that as a part -- assuming that this was possible to achieve, then, of course, the second stage was how to move from Plan B back to some sort of Plan A. That is an implementation on the ground. And then one was going to force the Pale leadership to do that. An element of that was that President Milosevic had to agree to further tightening of the ordered existing sanctions received against Republika Srpska. Those were essentially the three elements of what I referred to as the Plan B.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Plan B, what was Milosevic's position with regard to those three elements that you have mentioned about the plan as well as the tightening of further sanctions?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, we had rather extensive -- not only me, by the way. I mean, these negotiations had been initiated by the US diplomat, Robert Fraser who had been representing the contact groups in rather extensive talks with President Milosevic all through the spring of 1995. I think they solved most of the problems, although not all, but then there were some divisions inside the contact group and in the different countries so it was not carried to fruition. And Ambassador Fraser stepped down for a number of reasons and I took over, but, of course, there were extensive discussions on all of these three issues. I mean the, as I think the Tribunal is aware of, the devil is always in the details. And here it was the details that were more difficult than the overall scheme. The overall scheme was easier, but the details were extremely heartily fought over for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just intervene here. Exactly when did the Plan B start and for what was its duration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If -- I mean, this was said before I entered but I read -- tried to re-read my book on the flight down. Earlier of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early 1995, yes, after the -- because there had been effectively been no peace attempts after the collapse of the contact group plan in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So then this was another attempt, another way around the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So Plan B went from early 1995 to the end of the war to the Dayton --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's debatable because a lot of things happened during the latter part of the summer, of course. You can say that what happened, if you speak in terms of the plans, that we effectively collapsed Plan B and Plan A into what became Dayton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or Plan B did also collapse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no collapse in the sense of merge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, fair enough. Are you able to say more or less when it collapsed or when it merged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you can say that it merged with the intensified efforts that were initiated after both Srebrenica and Operation Storm, which was -- because from -- for a number of reasons. We saw a deterioration in the situation, of course, escalation of fighting -- well, earlier than that, as a matter of fact. And the summer of 1995 was, in my opinion, the worst period of the war after the initial period of the Bosnian war, which was in 1992. There was a number of reasons for this and we need not go into that. And then for other reasons that are related to other factors on the international scene, there was an acceleration of the efforts, in that it was necessary to bring the parties together. I would say that the critical meeting in these respects was the meeting that took place in Geneva at some -- between the -- all of the foreign ministers of the region at the date that I can't remember at the moment. That is in all of the records, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a procedural point. Could I -- I see Mr. Bildt is referring to his book. I have a copy of his book with me. When Mr. Bildt is refreshing his recollection, if he finds some point in the book that refreshes his recollection, it would be of assistance to me and to the parties if he could identify the page on which he has found the point that refreshes his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. And another procedural point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I concur with that. I have no difficulty with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The other procedural issue here, Mr. Guy-Smith, is that a witness is really expected to testify from memory and at each time there's a need for refreshing memory there should be a clear indication that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarification so we're sure that we're all on the same page. Are you reading from the Swedish version right now or from the English version so in case we need to refer to it, we can go to the right page number?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you so much. Now, contained -- contained in your answer there was one point that was, I believe, missing which was Milosevic's response to the plan itself. The three components of Plan B as well as the tightening of sanctions that had previously imposed, was he in accord with that or was he in disagreement with that?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall that I -- without going back in -- in the -- in the documents or the book and recall every single aspect of the negotiations but I said we negotiated every single detail was difficult to negotiate with him. Needless to say, these were difficult issues. As to the overall recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was okay with him. But he linked that, of course, to the agreement on the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was, needless to say, a somewhat controversial issue. Eventually we ended up with the wording that you see reflected in the communique coming out of the Geneva meeting that I -- that I referred to, and that was then directly taken into -- sort of fleshed out, you can say, in Dayton. I think the 49, 51 principle he grudgingly agreed to. As to the -- what was called the Drina blockade, that was not necessarily one of the issues that we spent the most time on. It was already in effect. But we discussed further tightening of it in different respects. It was somewhat difficult to tighten but anyhow there might have been different ways that you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I notice the noticeable absence of one name from -- from your discussion and I mention the name and then I want to go back to the issue of meeting Mladic on July 7th. But I noted the notable absence of the name of President Karadzic from your discussion.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: There was the reason that I mentioned, that after the collapse of the contact group plan, which had been on the take it or leave it basis, it was said, If you don't accept it, we're not going have contact with you. The policy was not to have contact with President Karadzic. So there was no contacts. I had one telephone conversation with him during the entire period that I was involved in the Balkans. But we had no -- I had no contacts with him whatsoever. There were other contacts with him but they were not by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you're referring to the 7th of July, 1995, when you say the name of President Karadzic is not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the negotiations that are extant throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the answer that you have just given, which is that the policy was not to have contact with President Karadzic, could you identify for us whose policy that was? And I will use the term internationals generically, but I don't know whether that is necessarily accurate for purposes of the decision that was being made after his refusal to take -- to take up the contact group plan in the initial instance.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No, it -- this was essentially the policy of the contact group. There were, however, other contacts. I think that during the summer there was a contact from -- I think, the Russian Federation sent an envoy to Pale at some point in time. So there were exceptions to the rule, but from our side, we were sort of conducting negotiations at the time. We didn't not have any contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I might ask then who were the parties to the negotiations under the auspices of this contact group. The reason I'm asking you is you say you had no contact with Karadzic. And my question would be: Who represented the Republika Srpska in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because the idea, which was later, sort of that was the way Dayton was done. The idea was to have an agreement with President Milosevic and then for President Milosevic to use all of the powers at his disposal to impose that settlement on the Pale leadership. And at the end of the day, that is what also happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it was an indirect approach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the contact group was really not a facilitator for negotiations. It came with a plan. It imposed it on everybody --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it tried to but failed. Because, I mean, that was the idea in the summer of 1993, I think, yeah, end of the first year. But when the plan was put on the table, you can -- historians could discuss whether that was a particular perfect plan, and I might have my views but that is a separate issue, but since that did not fly, then we had a stalemate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to break out of that stalemate, then what I consider -- what I refer to as Plan B, which was to use Milosevic in order to impose the settlement on the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for purposes my question, I'm really not interested in what whether it was a good or bad plan. What I want to know is how it was put in place. You've been using a "take it or leave it" phrase in describing it. You have now used the word "impose," but you are also saying, no, it was not something that the contact group brought and said you take it and you shall have it, whether you like it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was the case in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then when we come to 1994 and the autumn and the Geneva Dayton process, as you're aware of, the negotiations in Dayton was a negotiation with President Milosevic. There was no sort of Republika -- there was some Republika Srpska -- there was one Republika Srpska representative or person on the delegation of President Milosevic in Dayton. But then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Dayton is post-Plan B? It's post-contact group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: my question is really related to contact group. In the contact group phase, there was really no question of negotiation. It was, You want to take it, if you don't want to take it, we've got no contact with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we -- with the Bosnian Serb leadership, yeah, quite. We had no negotiations or contact with the Bosnian Serb leadership during that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You had contact with Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And -- yes. And should be added for the sake of clarity, I mean, President Tudjman in Zagreb because at this particular -- to get the entire picture although it gets complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of the drama was associated with Republika Srpska Krajina which eventually went into Operation Storm, which was another of the major events. So I would say that even if a lot of our focus is now on sort of the eastern front of Bosnian war, I would argue that at the time there was even more attention on the western front, of the drama there, involving also the Croats. And then President Tudjman was a key actor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. but the point I want to establish is that during the contact group period everybody else was represented but Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I want to note for the record that at page 17, starting at line 16, part of Mr. Bildt's answer was not recorded. The question that was put to Mr. Bildt was: Whose policy was it not to have contact with President Karadzic? And Mr. Bildt, I recorded in my notes, answered: It was the policy of the contact group. What is recorded at line 17 is the remainder of Mr. Bildt's answer and absent from that answer is that it was the policy of the contact group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are referring to line?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 17, line 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You confirm that that was part of your answer, Mr. Bildt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was it lost on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't follow the transcript so I don't know if it was lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but I assume it was lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. No, no, the question is: Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So we put it back on the transcript. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for everyone's comfort, my understanding is there always a transcript check and there's a manner by which all words are captured. And knowing the individual who is presently reporting, I know that's something that is done quite assiduously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But we always --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We always also thank the recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- just trying to get some ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just mention this little housekeeping matter in the middle of your examination, Mr. Guy-Smith, given that we started at an unusual time, the plan is that we'll break at quarter past 1.00 for a lunch break and come back at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We almost have Mladic arriving on the 7th of July. That's where we were moving towards. Did you have an opportunity to meet with General Mladic on the 7th of July Dobanovci in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now is this the first time that there has been contact with anybody in the leadership, be it political or military, of the Republika Srpska, since the initial contact group plan failed?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: It was my first contact. Whether -- and I said, to my knowledge, there had not been any contact between the UN command and General Mladic since May. Prior to that, of course, whether it had been with General Mladic or his different representatives, of course, there were fairly constant contact. But that is prior to my time, so you'll have to ask others about that. And then to make -- to go back to the original question, contact with the Republika Srpska, which we discussed, I mean, in some formal sense, well, more than formal, General Mladic was Republika Srpska. But when I refer to Republika Srpska, I refer to the Republika Srpska political leadership, de facto, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Should I then understand that while there was no contact with Karadzic, there was contact with Mladic during the contact group period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But that was of a different nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. He was the military leader.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... he was a military leader and the UN commander on the ground, and, of course, there had also been contacts on the humanitarian level. I mean, there were, as you are aware of, numerous UN agencies on the ground trying to help people, and they were in constant touch with other representatives in Pale and the Republika Srpska leadership. So when I refer to it, I refer to sort of full political talks with, de facto, Mr. Karadzic, who was in charge of that. And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And during that period did you meet Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean this is the first time which we are coming to now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you met General Mladic on the 7th of July, could you tell us what the nature of that conversation was? What were the topics that were discussed?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Page 53 is the -- the -- the description of the meeting and I have really nothing to add to it because this was 15 years ago, and what is written here I wrote down fairly immediately afterward. So this is a more accurate description that I have in the book than anything I can supply at the moment. The idea was, as said, to see if there was the possibility to re-establish a contact between the different military commands primarily in order to sort out of the supply situation for the enclaves. And among the enclaves, I would say that Sarajevo and Gorazde were the ones that were the focus of attention. And we had then asked President Milosevic whether it was possible to get in contact with General Mladic. President Milosevic said he wasn't certain but he was going try, and General Mladic turned out, if I remember it rightly, fairly late in the evening and claimed that he had come from far away. We assumed that was western Bosnia, but that was just an assumption since that was the military drama, and he was also fairly taken up by the military drama in the west at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll ask you since you referred to us page 53 --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say in the book and I wonder if this is -- refreshes your recollection as to what your intentions were at the time: "When darkness had descended over Dobanovci, another black car swept up to the large house and General Ratko Mladic climbed out, dressed completely in black. Milosevic had obviously called him. I let Mladic talk. I wanted to know his mindset." And then you go on, and you describe what you've described to us here in your oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like for you to take a look at the bottom of the page because you make a comment that: "He --"

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "-- lived in a narrow medieval world of injustices, revenge and continual struggles." Are you referring to your view of Mladic's --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah. This is my -- these were my impressions at the time of General Mladic. He spoke time and again about, quote, his people, as he were some sort of medieval warlord. And my enduring impression of our first meeting was that this was just what he was. "He lived in a narrow medieval world of injustices, revenge and continuous struggle. For him peace seemed to be an alien concept. No more than a truce in an everlasting struggle against the injustices to which history and the rest of the world had subjected his Serb people." That was how I interpreted the mindset of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the context of that particular mindset, what progress did you make on the 7th, in your estimation, with regard to the issues at hand?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, not -- not much has to be said. What he talked at the time, of course, and I think I'm now 53 or 54, anyhow, but around there, he wanted to -- he wanted to have a cease-fire which was fairly natural. I mean, he was sitting on 70 per cent of the territories. It would be fairly natural that he wanted to have that. He wanted to have a contact with the command of the ABiH for direct military to military talks. That was not possible for a number of reasons. I very much made the point to him as well as to President Milosevic, needless to say, who was present, during -- because I had spent some time with Milosevic prior to that, because we spent quite some time waiting to see if Mladic was going to turn up. Impressing on them that in order for there to be an end of the war, there had to be a calming down of fighting, no fighting on the ground because any further fighting would seriously disrupt the political process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: And also I stressed to him to try to -- I stressed the need of military restraint on the ground. It was inhuman, I stressed to him, to try to strangle Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Bihac. He did not object but asked why the UN did nothing to stop what the Croat army was doing along the Dinara mountains. I remember that. He kept coming back to Dinara all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This leaves you, I think, in somewhat of an interesting situation and you said he did not object. Did he indicate to you that he agreed with your general notion of what I will call for -- for the purposes of our discussion in a cease-fire or a stopping? And I'm talking about orally. A stopping of military movement? Were you left the impression after the 7th that Mladic was going to stop?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Fairly obviously. I mean he was sitting on -- I think he was still sitting on 70 per cent of the terrain. I'm not quite certain at that particular stage. The tide of the war had turned. And another thing that was fairly vivid in the debate at the time was that he was, of course, suffering or Republika Srpska was suffering under the impact of the Drina sanctions. They also faced -- I forgot the sort of population divisions, but, I mean -- but he had very difficulties to get the manpower to man his very long defensive lines. He was trying to get recruits from Yugoslavia proper in order to man the lines. The lines were long. They were thin. They were under pressure. So it's fairly obvious that he was very keen on a cease-fire at that particular time in order to sort of consolidate what he already had, which was essentially what he got in -- with a few exceptions, essentially what he acquired or taken control over in the beginning, in the first year of the war in 1992, when his forces were in [indiscernible]. But then the tide of the war turned and he saw that things were going in another direction. So what he said was, from the purely military point of view, fairly logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After your meeting on the 7th, both with Milosevic and with Mladic, my understanding is that you left the region for but a moment and flew out on the Saturday, the 8th.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At which point you had a series of meetings with various individuals. I think perhaps including Richard Holbrooke. I don't know whether any of those are critical to our discussion right now but I want to keep us in a chronological order. There was some discussion, however, I believe, with regard to the status of UNPROFOR and the continued involvement of UNPROFOR in the region that was occurring. And I --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, the first two sentences of -- that must refer to the first two sentences on page 55, which just refer to the fact that on July the 8th, there was report from UNPROFOR in Zagreb to UN headquarters in New York. So it's the fact that there was a regular UN report on that particular day. Nothing that had anything to do with me. I just know of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also note the fact on page 54, at the bottom of the page, that threat of UNPROFOR withdrawal --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to this manner of proceeding. I think we should proceed on a question and answer basis. I find Mr. Bildt's book quite interesting but I don't think it is productive to sit and refer to various parts of the book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and read the book. So we if could proceed in the normal fashion, which is ask questions. If Mr. Bildt needs to refresh his recollection, he can refer to the book and he can inform the parties that he needs to refresh his recollection, and then we can proceed from that way. But I think we evolved into a system now where we are just reading the book and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll back away from that system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I had referred to that earlier too. And while there is this interruption. Mr. Bildt, I'm not quite sure that your answer was captured as I thought I heard it. At page 26, line 13, if you can look on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 26, line 13 -- page 26 has just disappeared. But it's line 13. Well, the first two sentences -- that must refer to the first two sentences on 55, which just referred to the fact that on July 8th, there was report from UNPROFOR in Zagreb to UN headquarters. I thought you did tell us what the report was about but it's not captured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But I said we were now really into sort of fairly peripheral facts. It's just the fact that there was a regular UN report. For some reason I have noted that in my book. I have no -- I was not involved in any sort of way, and since I got a question, I referred to the book and I read from the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I failed to see that this has any relevance to the case, I have to confess, but that is my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the question that's put to you. Okay. If -- to the extent possible, if you can just put the book aside and try to answer the questions from counsel, and if you do need to refresh your memory from the book, you are obviously allowed to do so, but at that point everybody in court needs to know that you are now referring to the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now going to move from the 8th to the 11th of July. With regard to the 11th of July would it help refresh your recollection with regard to those events if you refer to your book or do you have an independent recollection sufficient at this time to be able to give us a response?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, I don't have a sufficient independent recollection so anything I would say without referring to the book would be substantially less reliable than relying on the book. I mean, that's -- because these were events and it was a very sort of rapid sequence of events so -- and the book does record them fairly detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that in mind, referring now to the 11th of July, do you recall on the 11th of July who you were with and where you were travelling from or to?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I wouldn't recall it if I hadn't re-read it in the book earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Having re-read it earlier in the book today, is your recollection refreshed as you sit here right now?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was going from Geneva, I think, to Strasbourg for meetings that had been planned. That was meetings -- there was a meeting happening in Strasbourg at the time between President Chirac of France, Chancellor Kohl of Germany. I recollect having meetings with Chancellor Kohl but that was on separate issues, nothing do with the Bosnian war, and later with President Chirac. And then I had a meeting with the foreign minister of Bosnia, Mr. Sacirbegovic. Or Sacirbey [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the 11th, what information, if any, had you received with regard to the situation militarily in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, during the 11th, when we were in Strasbourg, in the European Parliament or the then buildings of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, we received through the newswires information about the fall of Srebrenica. The situation there had been heating up during the -- really since the Friday, if I remember, the date of that, I can't remember that, but that is easy to find in the calendar. And I remember also having sent a message to President Milosevic on the 10th, I think, a direct message to him saying that he should be aware that any moves in terms of Srebrenica would have seriously detrimental effects on the political situation and could endanger the entire peace efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the representations that had been made to you on the 7th by General Mladic, with regard to the issue of continued military action, how did you interpret General Mladic's statements to you on the 7th when on the 11th you learned that, in fact, there had been a continued military action?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I don't interpret. I just note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You just note?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you just note, what did you note in that regard as it related to the statements made to you and assurances given to you by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, that evidently things were happening on ground. That is why we sent this message to -- or I sent the message to President Milosevic with a very clear warning to him on the 10th. If I remember it rightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, had General Mladic made any assurances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He had not -- he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned any assurances, did I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's in the question. It's in the question. It comes in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not -- it's in his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair, going back to the 7th now, based upon previous response, would it be fair that after your conversation with Mladic on the 7th, that you came away from that meeting with assurances from Mladic that there would no further military activity? I understand your analysis with regard to the fact that he had 70 per cent of the region.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. I did not have any such impression, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based upon your conversations with Mladic on the 7th, were you comfortable in the notion that there would be no further military activity?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I mean, I wasn't confident with anything at that particular stage, I have to be quite honest, because we were in a situation where things were deteriorating by the day in different parts of theatre. As said, from roughly whatever, May or something, May, June, we were in a situation of rapid deterioration of both the military and the political situation. I wasn't comfortable with anything. We were busy trying to sort of calm things down and trying to restart the political process, but we were not confident about anything, not comfortable with anything and things were going from bad to worse by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now with regard to the situation on the 11th, did a new factor come into consideration with regard to the international response to Mladic's attack on Srebrenica? And by that I'm referring to NATO or the use of any kind of air support.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, obviously, I mean, the fall of Srebrenica changed the entire equation because this was the first time any of the sort of enclaves had been attacked and fallen. It had obviously very severe both political and humanitarian repercussions, although the humanitarian ones were -- turned out to be far worse than anyone was aware of at the time. But it was bad as it was. Srebrenica had been the subject of acute concerns ever since back to 1993 again, I think, when the safe areas were established. So it was, of course, a major event, a major further erosion of the overall situation that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to back up for a minute. Before you took this post, enviable or unenviable as it may be, in retrospect, were you briefed with regard to the history of the negotiations and the historical situation that had occurred on the ground from 1993?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I was briefed on the political negotiations, yes, not necessarily on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have any information with regard to the concerns that had existed in previous years, both militarily as well as from a humanitarian standpoint?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: On Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, I had prime minister of my country. I had received I think 150.000 refugees. I had been receiving them nearly on a daily basis. I fought an election campaign in my country defending their rights to come to the country. I was acutely aware of the suffering in Bosnia, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm -- I'm asking you the question is because I want to make sure that we have an understanding of not only the level of your sophistication with regard to the issues that were of immediate concern but also the history and your awareness of the history of the region in that particular time, so we understand what you were juggling with while, as you've put it, these events were unfolding and rapidly deteriorating. With regard to the 11th of July, were any requests made to you to use air power in reaction to Mladic's overtaking of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. Not that I can recollect. Why should they? I didn't have an aircraft of my own even. I mean, I was not in any sort of military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: The chain of command for the UN forces was a UN chain of command, and I was not in the UN. I was the European Union. The UN was, of course, separate. Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Akashi, Mr. Rupert Smith, and add to that, of course, when it comes to air power they have a separate arrangement with NATO and a separate chain of command. But I was not in either of those chains of commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned on the 11th that you had meetings with Muhamed Sacirbey, the foreign minister, Sacirbey. Did you get any indication from him what his reaction to was -- his reaction was to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: We spent most of -- it was a rather short meeting I had with him because obviously we were both running off in different directions. That focussed to a very large extent on the need to get humanitarian help. Because obviously lots of people and it was a question of their faith and it was a question of helping them to de facto get out. This was the subject of subsequent talks that I had also with President Izetbegovic, because that was a somewhat sensitive issue, to help them with the evacuation. But that was the -- primarily what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have heard testimony that you told an individual on the day that Srebrenica fell, that Srebrenica also Zepa and Gorazde would not be defended if they came under attack. Did you ever make such a statement?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. I mean, at that time Srebrenica had fallen. So I couldn't have made such a statement because that was -- had already happened. Gorazde, of course, we did somewhat later try to defend or at least threaten to defend or to be precise tried to deter attack on with air power. Although whether that would have worked was debatable in my opinion. Zepa was a separate story which is much more complicated. But as I referred to in our conversation with Milosevic and Mladic on the 7th, we were very clear in our messages that they should respect the rights, if you call them rights, of the -- of all of the enclaves, and you had the three eastern enclaves. Sarajevo was also an enclave, you should not forget. This was a period when the isolation of Sarajevo was among the tightest it had been during the entire war period and we should neither forget Bihac, which is also very isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. Understood. With regard to your conversations with Mr. Sacirbey, did he indicate to you that Srebrenica was or was not a problem?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I mean, needless to say, Srebrenica was a problem. It was a major challenge both for the international community and for everyone else because there was -- don't remember, 30.000, 40.000 people or something like that under absolutely appalling humanitarian circumstances, as well as a lot of other problems associated with it which had to do with the inner dynamics of Sarajevo. And it was a major concern in terms also of the supply of the UN forces there because, as you're aware of, there had been -- I mean, the UN forces had not been supplied for quite some time, if I remember it rightly, so they were low on virtually everything. So it was one of the major concerns. If it was the one, I don't know. But it was one of the major concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the effect that a peace negotiation or ultimate peace settlement would have with respect to Srebrenica, did he voice to you his position with regard to what would happen once peace was obtained?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, I -- going back to Your Honours' question about what I remember and what's in the book, I have sort of very little recollections. There is something in the book which I might refer to but I have no independent recollections after 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you would take an opportunity to take an opportunity to take a look at your book --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- read it and tell us what page are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I think I'm on 56, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May I suggest 57.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: You may suggest 57. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could counsel please switch off his microphone when not asking questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I write here something about his reaction, that he was somewhat calmer than even me. It might be that he had been following the situation on the ground more closely than I had been. He said that they knew that a peace settlement would mean the loss of the enclave. Whether that is true or not, I don't know. Ask him. But then he was deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation, appealed for as much active assistance as possible to evacuate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Bildt please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I could. He appealed for as much active assistance as possible to evacuate the refugees and to help him in this very difficult situation. I eagerly promised to do whatever I could in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I note the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will take the break until quarter past 2.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the staff must go for lunch. They have been in court for the whole morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- I -- just to urge you that I have sort of fairly urgent at some point -- I'm happy to be here, no question about, but I have some sort of fairly urgent government business awaiting me in Stockholm as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Bildt. But the other problem is that, as you may see or have been taught, the tape goes one and a quarter hours and then they need some time to -- to clean that and we've got to come back. As you might have heard Mr. Guy-Smith referring to corrections that are made, so during the break they make corrections, we come back. That's how it operates here, and unfortunately, using -- given the technology we use here, we can't do it otherwise. So we will take a break and come back at quarter past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, before -- before we start, I have been -- I have been asked to speak up and speak more slowly, and it's also been asked that you speak also a bit more slowly, especially when you're reading, because you have a tendency to speed up, as we all do. So if we could just keep that in mind, I think that we then might avoid some of the interruptions that we've had thus far and we'd make a number of the staff much happier and we'd have a more complete record. With that in mind, I'd like to know whether or not you ever engaged in discussions or approached anyone concerning the trade of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo as a solution or as a part of the peace settlement process.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. The eastern enclaves, no. As you -- there obviously had been a lot of discussion during the course of the negotiations on the territorial question. May I remind you that I was brought in early June of 1995. My focus, what I was asked to do was really to negotiate some of the political aspects of it. I did not go into, neither had I the mandate to go into, the territorial issues. They came, of course, to the forefront somewhat later, when we approached Dayton, when it was a question of sorting out of map. I mean, to decide what was the 49 and 51, and was then the subject of rather intense discussions in Dayton. There was also -- but that was not me. There was also, of course, a subsequent American attempt to present some sort of preliminary map, but I was never involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have previously heard testimony that, with regard to the trade of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo, that an individual was approached. He never initiated, and he would have, he was approached by you with regard to the concept of trade of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo [sic]. Is that statement an accurate or true statement, that you approached any individuals?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Whom should I have approached?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, put it in -- in these terms. That during the time that you were involved with negotiations concerning the peace settlement, you have mentioned a number of individuals that you spoke with.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am constrained by certain procedural rules from mentioning any specific names. So the question is: Do you have any independent recollection of ever dealing with, for example, anybody of the Republika Srpska side in which you approached them with regard to the issue of trading the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo? Let's start with that and then I will go through each group.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, as said, we did not have -- go back to what we said earlier, during this particular phase we didn't have any contacts of that sort --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: -- with the representatives of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now with regard to the Bosnia-Herzegovina side, did you ever approach any individuals on the Bosnia-Herzegovina side with regard to the same issue, once again that being --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No, because we were -- as said, my focus was on the political part of the settlement, which was the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while sort of the territorial issues which had been dealt with with the contact group map, summer of 1993, was left aside for the time being. They were later to resurface, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the 51, 49?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 59, 41 [sic]. And how to implement, sort of, that particular thing. That was the focus of a lot of the Dayton talks, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I want to take us up to the 14th of July, if I could.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And ask you if you can recall, as you sit here today, where you were on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in Belgrade from somewhere for a subsequent meeting with, among others, President Milosevic. I'd had number of scheduled meetings with him fairly frequently as part of the negotiation, so this was the next scheduled meeting that was going take place, on Friday, the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the meeting on the 14th of July, can you tell us who else was present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: There were a series of meetings during the 14th and the 15th, which quite certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: -- you're aware of. And my recollection might not be perfect on exactly the sequence of different meetings but I think that it started with me meeting -- well, it started with me having other meetings of the diplomatic community, and in Belgrade having contact with Washington and with other places to prepare for -- because we were then in a completely different situation that had to do with the fall of Srebrenica. So it was a question of internationally calibrating the message that we're going to give to President Milosevic. But as -- then I assume that my meeting with President Milosevic was the same format as usual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me interrupt me just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, if you can come closer to the microphone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And be slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And be slower. If you look at that screen, the stenographer says can you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Yes, the different meetings on July 14th and 15th. Arriving in Belgrade, I had the reason to coordinate with the international community and I used the diplomatic facilities available to me to communicate with key capitals, notably Washington, because we were then in a completely new situation after the fall of Srebrenica. Then my meeting with President Milosevic, which I think was in Dobanovci as usual, I would assume. I have no recollection of anyone else from the Yugoslav side, I'd say, than the individuals that we mentioned previously being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That being the individual you've identified as Goran?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Yes, I would have remembered if there were -- and if I remember it rightly, there was is no one else mentioned in my book that would have been. Then, subsequently, at some point in time we had General Mladic again. And then during the 15th, we had for follow-up meetings, of course, quite an elaborate procedure of international representatives. The UN SRSG, Mr. Akashi; the UN Special Envoy, Mr. Stoltenberg; the commander UN BH command, General Rupert Smith; and from my staff, General de Lapresle and General Elliot. And there might well have been others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to meetings that were held on 15th of July, do you recall whether or not an agreement was made or working points were obtained between General Smith and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, there was a preliminary agreement made which was to be ratified at a meeting a week later between General Mladic and General Rupert Smith, which related to both access to Srebrenica, which was to go into effect immediately, and access to the enclaves. This was the first meeting between the Generals since at least May. And accordingly, on the 15th, there was a rather lengthy and very heated discussion between the Generals on both the situation, what had happened and how to proceed. And there was the preliminary agreement along the lines that I indicated to be formalised at the meeting I think a week later that subsequently took place somewhere, in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have P2369 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The document -- yes, it is with us now.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a look at this Prosecution exhibit, if you would.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which consists, I believe, of three pages in total. Yes. And in terms of -- in terms of, first of all, the first page, is that the meeting that you were referring to that occurred on the 15th? Or one of the meetings that -- let me rephrase that question. One of the meetings that you were referring to that occurred on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah. This is obviously the cable from Mr. Akashi to the then-head of peacekeeping, Mr. Kofi Annan, in New York, that refers to meeting on Saturday, July the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is -- you were discussing, as I think -- if I'm not mistake, there was a long meeting between the two Generals, that being General Smith and General Mladic. They had not met for some time. And you mentioned that some informal agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's something else that's indicated on the first page with regard to the presence of Mladic at these meetings. Could you share with us what the decision was with regard to it being made public whether Mladic was involved or present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, if we go to the second page of this particular document, which I recollect, it says -- yes. You read there in the beginning, the specified agreement will be revealed of the meeting with General Mladic and General Smith scheduled for Wednesday, the 19th of July. For some reason which had to do with internal dynamics on the Serb side, they wanted to have this in the public domain a week later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the determination was made that it would not be in the public domain on the 15th. Mladic's presence was being kept secret at that time for some reasons.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, most of the meetings -- yeah. There was no press release on most of this, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since we are on -- on the second page, and looking at the very top, it says understandings from Belgrade discussion situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then there are a series of issues that are -- as I understand it, the informal agreement that was made at that time as between General Mladic and General Smith.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, that is correct.
