utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the Srebrenica portion of the understandings.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph down, which discusses that the ICRC shall have immediate access to "prisoners of war," to assess their welfare and register and review procedures at Bosnian Serb reception centre in accordance with the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is there any further information that you can give us with regard to this particular aspect of the informal agreement that was had between Mladic and Smith? Was this --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No. With the exception that, concerning Srebrenica, the informal agreement, which I don't know if that is specified in this particular document, was that this should go into force immediately. And there was set up, if I remember it rightly, some sort of point of contact for the UN on the VRS side to arrange this. I think it was General -- was it Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gvero?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah. Whether it was UNHCR to get in touch with him or whatever, I can't remember. But the UN contact with General Gvero that should happen fairly immediately in order to implement these particular aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: If it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It maybe sound a bit foolish and I don't mean it to be, but with regard to the understanding of -- to have access to prisoners of war, what would the -- what would that entail in a practical sense?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: You will have to ask ICRC and others because they had their particular channels and I was not prior -- I was not informed about everything. ICRC has a specific mandate and a specific role and they had their specific channels and my role here, as indicated earlier, I was responsible for the political talks. It was just that since the military to military and other links had been broken down, I was just facilitating these particular meetings and contacts at that particular time. But the ones who were dealing with these issues was UNHCR, obviously, but also ICRC. When it comes to what was defined as prisoners of war, that was a controversial issue in itself, how you define a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what the controversy was there as between Generals Mladic and Smith?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Not the -- I'm not aware of any controversy on this particular point that you ask now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: They had a rather profound disagreement on the nature of the war, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm specifically interested in the topic which is entitled "Cessation of hostilities" for the first moment. Which is -- it says here: "Serbs propose that all generals commanding warring parties be invited, in the presence of Mr. Bildt, to discussions on a cessation of hostilities agreement." I take it that was something to happen in the future. And when it says "Serbs propose" here, is that referring to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I think we alluded to this earlier. This was a fairly standard -- I don't know what he wants, but standard request by General Mladic. As said, he, for reasons that I indicated, had an interest in closing down the war. He was sitting on 70 per cent of the territory. The tide of the war was turning, fairly obvious. He wanted to have a direct link with General Delic, commanding general of the BiH, and sit down with him and agree on this, and he wanted to us facilitate that. That was obviously a distinct non-start because, as you quite certain are aware of, at that particular point in time, there was a breakdown between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic. I'm not aware of how they were communicating, if they were commuting at all. There was an acute political conflict between them, which is extremely obvious and extremely public. So Mladic was operating from that point of view. Uncertain how much but quite independently. While, of course, General Delic was in a completely different situation. In Sarajevo these issues, the detailed issues were dealt with by the political leadership, while, on the VRS side, Mladic was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the details were dealt with by the political leadership, on the -- with regard to the BiH, I take it you're referring to the political leadership at that time being President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: The Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The Presidency.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: The Presidency which was headed by President Izetbegovic. So it was no question of them allowing, for good reasons in my opinion, sort of the direct talks between General Mladic and General Delic. Although that was what Serbs wanted, for reasons that are fairly obvious, or the VRS wanted for reasons that were fairly obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to satisfy my curiosity here. Given the breakdown of relations between Mladic and Karadzic and to your communication with Mladic, what hope was there of implementing any agreement that might have come about between Mladic on the one hand and any other party supposing Delic came, for one reason or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do think that any meeting between Mladic and Delic would have been a distinct non-start because the issues were essentially political at this particular phase. So it had to be political agreement on how to settle the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask my question slightly differently. Given this breakdown, what was the basis for your pursuing negotiations with Mladic as a party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we did not negotiate with Mladic as a party. We negotiated with Milosevic. He was our party to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he keeps on bringing Mladic to whatever meetings you are having.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, not to whatever meetings. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had extensive meetings with Milosevic. We're just talking twice. And that was at our request in order to facilitate the re-establishment of the military to military contact, which was between the UN and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, the UN forces were, of course -- they were to some extent in between, as we know, so they were in need of constant communication with the three armies on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to this exhibit that's on the screen, Mladic is featuring quite a lot. There are lots of discussions between him and General Smith. And in response to your question about the Serbs proposing that all Generals commanding warring parties being invited, you -- I think you said that Mladic was the guy who was making this demand, because he was sitting on 70 per cent. This war was turning against him and -- so it seems to me as if Mladic is the main player.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the military side he was, on the Bosnian Serb side, yes. Then our -- to be quite frank, at the time we could only note the conflict that was there between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. We saw it in the Bosnian Serb media and at some point in time, I can't remember when, of course, Mr. Karadzic sort of dismissed General Mladic as commander of the VRS. That -- and Mr. Karadzic appeared in uniform on the streets of Banja Luka. He made himself a laughing stock by doing that because it was obvious that the army units were responding to General Mladic and not to Mr. Karadzic. But the exact nature of the relationship was, of course, unknown to us at the time. I'm quite certain that the different documents available to the Tribunal today would shed light on that. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at that particular time, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have that light. I was just interested in -- if I'm -- and I'm not being disrespectful here because I'm just trying to be as clear as I possibly can, what you hoped achieve by -- and when by you, not you personally, the group that was negotiating -- the group that is mentioned on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or simply because he is a military head he could impose his will on the political leadership, maybe was that the expectation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not for this. He was in command of what was the acute issue from the UN military side. I was facilitating those contacts, as I said. I was not primarily doing them. But the acute situation that was there was, of course, the situation of the enclaves. And when we talked about the enclaves, the enclave that was really acute was Sarajevo. I mean, Milosevic was sitting on the supply lines and he was denying the resupply of all of the enclaves and he was tightening the siege of Sarajevo. And, of course, apart from the humanitarian concerns which were foremost in our minds, I mean, the population was suffering heavily, this was -- and I remember in Sarajevo they were heading for the third or the fourth winter of war at that particular time. It was also the resupply of the UN forces that were in the different enclaves, including in Sarajevo. And I don't know if that is reflected here in the document, but the most vivid discussion was concerning the resupply of Sarajevo, where we had managed to get agreement to open up the land access with some limitations, because up until that time he had closed all land access, and we and the UN had been dependant upon the -- both unreliable, very limited and very dangerous route over the Igman, with all of the problems associated with that. Here we got agreement to open the road from Kiseljak into Ilidza. Although, as I think is somewhere in the documents as well, the critical issue was supply of ammunition, where Mladic was adamant in his use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to interrupt. Just at page 47, line 10, I'm not sure if that name is the correct name that was correctly reported. I heard that name but I'm not sure Mr. Bildt intended that to be the name and so I'd just like to clarify that part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see that Mr. Bildt? Page 47, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where it says -- I will read it, if you'd like. It says: "When we talked about the enclaves, the enclave that was really acute was Sarajevo. Milosevic was sitting on the supply lines ..." And I'm not sure and just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mladic was sitting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladic was sitting on supply lines. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did see it and I was wondering and I thought -- but either could fit. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since His Honour has focussed somewhat on the relationship as between Milosevic and Mladic and Mladic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I focus between Mladic and Karadzic. That was my focus. Not Milosevic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since the Chamber's -- excuse me. Since the Chamber's focus was on Mladic and Karadzic and necessarily with -- within that becomes another issue which is the relationship between Milosevic and Mladic, I'd like to discuss with you whether or not on the 14th specifically, you had any indications of the ability of Milosevic to control Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, I -- "control" is a word that one can discuss in different terms. But I vividly remember where he was not able to do it, and that was the issue that I indicated. That is the supply of ammunition. Because we had a need to get [indiscernible] from the humanitarian things into Sarajevo, I mean, food, everything that is needed for supply of city. People were having very, very difficult situation. Supply of the UN forces with everything you need. I can't remember how many thousands there were but substantial numbers anyhow in Sarajevo. But the critical issue was ammunition. They were running low on certain ammunitions. And Milosevic -- sorry, Mladic took heavy -- after a while he agreed that we could open up supply lines again. But he would not allow lethal -- that is ammunition to the UN forces to come in. He took particularly -- and I think that was caused by the fact that at that time the UN forces had begun to be in certain respects rather tough. There had been deployed, I can't remember exactly when, but some French heavy mortars with artillery locating radars as well, which means that there was the possibility certainly to do counter-battery fire, which had not been the case before. And there had been, I think it is in my book somewhere, case where this counter-battery fire had been deployed with devastating effect, and that had impacted upon him and he did not want to have this particular battery resupplied with ammunition. I mean, perfectly logical from his point of view. But we were, of course, insisting on that because the UN -- we had the UN, UN had the right, Security Council resolutions, whatever legality, was completely on our side. We demanded the right to resupply the forces with whatever the forces needed. On this particular point Milosevic tried to say to Mladic, You have to agree with this. The situation is such you have agree to it. But I'm not -- I can't recollect exactly what was the resolution of the issue because that went into the subsequent meetings between General Rupert Smith and General Mladic and I was not prior to the resolution of that particular conflict. But it was a fairly lively one, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did you -- it is not a question of Milosevic gives an order and Mladic carries it out. It was a question of negotiation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a question of Milosevic saying, "I think we should do this." And on quite a number of issues you see Mladic saying, "Yes, yes, yes," but there were limits to it. There were distinct limits to it at some times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I picked up right after the -- Judge Moloto asked you the question that you your first answer was no.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said -- he asked you the question which is not reflected in the transcript which is why I'm asking. He asked the question: It's not a question Milosevic gives an order and Mladic carries it out. It was a question of negotiation. I heard you saying no. Is that accurate, did you say no?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I don't know what I said. But -- but I wouldn't -- I wouldn't call it negotiation either because then you have sort of two independent parties negotiating. I mean, it was a complex relationship, and I was only subject to two conversations between the two men. So my knowledge of the relationship is somewhat limited. I had limited impressions from those. But I can say that on a certain part of that it was Milosevic said, This is the way it should be done or you ought to do, and he said okay. But on certain other cases, he said distinctly, No, I'm not going do it. And Milosevic could be quite firm against him and didn't really help. Although, I, as said, Your Honour, I don't know what was the final outcome of those particular issues but during the conversations that I was part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask this question. Are you able to recollect Mladic's response to Milosevic's statement that Mladic ought to allow weaponry to go through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not literally but effectively he was refusing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So effectively it didn't happen. He just didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I said, Your Honour, what eventually happened a couple of weeks later, or one week later, at the meeting between General Rupert Smith and General Mladic, I don't know. Whether the resupplied -- but then, of course, things changed fundamentally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you don't know what caused the change there but while you were there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It -- that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I get the sense from the number of interchanges we've had here that -- and I'm asking, would this be fair to say that there were limits to what Milosevic could get Mladic to accept?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: It is very difficult to me to make a generalised statement on such an issue because that is obviously a rather complex relationship with very many dimensions to it. I can only refer to the two meetings that I had, where the two meetings -- where the two men were at the same time and those were the only two times I met General Mladic ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it help refresh your recollection, with regards to the specific question that I asked you, to refer to your book where you talk about this? And that would be page 62. And starts with the second paragraph: "In general terms ..."

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah. No, that's -- yeah. Now I read it that is exactly what -- that's roughly what I've said here previously. In somewhat more literal language perhaps but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So is it your recollection that with regard to these discussions Milosevic was helpful?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Milosevic at that time was interested in -- in my opinion getting a deal fairly fast for reasons that we don't need to go into. He was aware of the fact that there was a very strong international reaction to the fall of Srebrenica. And obviously it was his interest to be helpful in order to moderate that international reaction. So he was helpful in trying to facilitate the document that you saw here, the exhibit. Then as a completely separate issue is, of course, to which extent that document was implemented. And we all know the facts concerning that. That's a later story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, if you could just read, if it is a short passage, that page 62 in general terms because we don't have a copy of your book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem. It's not your problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said in general terms Milosevic was helpful in these discussions. He knew how sensitive the Sarajevo issue was to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please read slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "He knew how sensitive the Sarajevo issue was to world opinion, but there were limits to what he could get Mladic to accept. When Milosevic joined me in pressing him to accept the complete freedom of the UN to resupply its force in Sarajevo, his face flushed dark red, he banged his fist on the table, stared at Milosevic and said he would never accept the bringing in of ammunition that the UN forces could use against his soldiers. And indeed, the UN forces in Sector Sarajevo had started to counter-attack with effect. The French heavy mortars were deadly in their accuracy ..." and that's roughly what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say Milosevic fell silent and beat a discrete --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that was the literary language, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- retreat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I now want to move from that time. We have a problem here which apparently we were overlapping and I wanted to just make sure the record is clear here. On line 11, apparently, we started speaking over each other. I said: "You say Milosevic fell silent and beat a discrete retreat." And I believe your response was that it was -- that's what your book says and it was a styled in a literary form. I'm using -- I may be paraphrasing your language but I believe that's what the two of us -- that's the meaning of that particular part of the conversation. And if I can get you to answer, because a nod doesn't come up on the --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I want to move now to the 19th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- didn't Mr. Bildt also mention that Mladic hit the table?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He did. Did that not come up either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It might have disappeared but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to the 19th of July, do you recall where you were on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: In Belgrade again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time, when you were in Belgrade, did you have occasion to meet Mladic again or have we now completed our meetings with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: We have now completed them because what has happened was that then the contact had been re-established between the military commanders, so at the same time I think there was the meeting between General Rupert Smith and General Mladic and the discussion on the -- sort of the on the ground issues were then back to the military to military, UN, VRS, ABiH level. And I was dealing solely with the political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now with regard to the situation in Srebrenica up until this point, the understanding is that there has been a military assault on the enclave which has been vigorously objected to, as I understand it, by you and the rest of the international community. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There have been efforts to obtain a cease-fire and an informal discussion has occurred in which there are a series of points, speaking points or actual agreements have been made between the two Generals that are supposed to take effect on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't necessarily say there had been efforts to obtain a cease-fire. Because clearly that was not in the cards at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: There had been -- General Mladic had expressed the view -- the wish for such a meeting in order to discuss that, but clearly for reasons that I have alluded to, that was not in the cards at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So then --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: At that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Mladic had in effect inserted a condition precedent to there being a cease-fire which is the meeting with Delic which you explained to us was not going to occur for a series of political reasons.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I wouldn't put too much emphasis on this because this was really -- I mean, these comments of him were really a side show. It passed by and it's a passing reference in my book only because I think he knew also that was a non-starter, as things were at that particular period of time. It sort of -- a couple of weeks later things were different but we were -- we are now in an extremely dynamic and dramatic situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: -- as to the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Now, I believe it's the next day that you learn for the first time about the events that you have termed and others have termed as being the massacres in Srebrenica, the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes. Depends on what you mean. Srebrenica were quite a number of events. I mean, we had the fall of it. We had the -- which I was involved in then, trying to get people out, and -- and that was, of course, primarily the women and the children. There was the convoys that were organised and the receptions at Tuzla airfield. There were a lot of problems associated with that that we had to deal with. Eventually that, as we know, happened. We were aware of the fact that there was a column trying to break through. I can't remember exactly when and how we got our detailed information about that, because things were obviously somewhat difficult to get information on what exactly was happening at that time. And then there were the fact that sort of the men had been separated. We knew that from the women coming out. And then, of course, I think on the 20th, the first indication that the men had not been kept in custody of -- but had been massacred or killed in large numbers. It was sketchy information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that information, if we were to take a look at the meeting on the 15th, in which a series of -- of negotiation points had been arrived at, was obviously directly contrary to anything that you -- that you had expected because there was, among other things, an understanding there would be access to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah, but I wouldn't use the word "expected." Because in the word "expectation" is the assumption that we believed everything that was said. At that time, my experience was perhaps not as extensive as later, but I was already aware of the fact that you should not necessarily take for granted that what people promised that they delivered. So the word "expectation" I wouldn't necessarily say. That did not prevent us from trying to get commitments by people because there was at least some possibility that they would implement some of it. But I can't really say that when we found out that it was not implemented, that that came as a complete bolt out of the blue and was out of the ordinary. I mean, there had been -- my knowledge of the previous negotiating history was that there had been, unfortunately, a lot of this before. That things being promised and things turned out otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just to back away just for a moment. You have been involved in negotiations, political negotiations, both at a domestic level and an international level for some many years now. And would it be fair to say that generally speaking with regard to the issue of negotiations and statements that are made in a negotiation process, that it is not necessarily the best thing in the world to rely on everything that is being said?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: That is somewhat dependant upon the situation. I wouldn't take that as a generalised statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the situation in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I wouldn't take that as a generalised statement on the Balkans either. But I noted that I would not use the word "expected" for the -- what you referred to earlier concerning this particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to representations that were made by General Mladic, would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: My only -- as said, I only had these two meetings in order to facilitate other contacts with him, so I never sort of went into sort of true negotiations with him or anything of that sort. But I noted that there were these -- you referred to the agreement that he concluded here or the whatever you call it, with the -- with the UN commanders on the ground, and we all know that those -- what he promised there, was not delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Primarily on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Was delivered on certain other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the situation and ultimately the information you received on the 20th of July concerning the massacres in Srebrenica, at that time based on all the information that you had, was the situation that occurred in Srebrenica foreseeable or not?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Which situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The massacres.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: The massacres or the genocide. I think I write in the book and I think that is still my view, that what happened in Srebrenica was even by the standards of the Balkan wars surprising. It was -- I mean, this was an extremely brutal war. I referred to -- my impression of General Mladic and sort of the medieval mindset, I wouldn't necessarily say that he was the only one with that medieval mindset when it comes to -- we have a concept of warfare in the west, for better or worse, that is that we nowadays make a distinction between armies and the population. That is the laws of the -- the laws of war. That didn't really apply. So there were horrendous war crimes committed throughout the war. I don't need to tell this here, by the way. But even by those standards I think what was happening in Srebrenica was unique in its barbarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did we expect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, was it foreseeable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have an answer to that. We -- we spent a long time afterwards trying to see -- or others spent a long time afterwards, but I'm aware that others spent a long time afterwards, where the intelligence was available, on the attack and the answer to a large extent was no. Was there the possibility of foreseeing what later happened? I don't know, frankly speaking. The only one that -- I think that's in the book as well, the one when I started in early July -- no, early June, the one who sort of was very worried about what might happen in Srebrenica was the Russian foreign minister, Andrey Kozyrev, and the reason for that, I think was the fact he had been Russian foreign minister for quite some time, so he had been involved in Srebrenica in 1993 and was perhaps more aware than many of the emotions and tensions surrounding that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to move a slightly different subject for the moment. And that deals with whether or not you ever had occasion to be at an airport where there were US air forces and Iranian aeroplanes delivering weaponry?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Weaponry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Aeroplanes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you expand on that a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What you did see; where were you?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I think referred to one instance where at Split airport I noted that lined up each -- beside each other was US Air Force that was delivering equipment, whatever it could have been, for the rapid reaction force that was coming in, and then there was an Iranian plane with, I understand, an Iranian delegation of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say an Iranian delegation, do you know what that Iranian delegation was in the midst of doing?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. After the information that you received on -- on the 20th - I'm going to move forward now - I understand there were a series of discussions with regard to potential use of air-strikes and a number of other matters that occurred. But I want to move now, if I could, to the 29th of July. 29th of July is a time when you received a, I believe, specific telephone call.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to get some understanding of what happened there, if we could.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I guess this refers to what is on page 69 and 70 of -- of my book. I was -- I was in Stockholm at the time and I received a telephone call from Mr. Muratovic, who I think was prime minister in Bosnia at the time, and he wanted to meet with me urgently in Split. I was on my way to see Chancellor Kohl in, I think, in Austria before, which I did. But when Mr. Muratovic wanted to see me urgently, I knew it was something important, particularly in view of the fact that he said we should meet in Split. And for him to go from Sarajevo to Split during the siege in the war was not an easy thing, to put it mildly. So it was something major that was obviously there. We met at the airport at some point in time, and the conversation was about Zepa. As you know the -- after -- after the fall of Srebrenica, the Bosnian Serb forces concentrated or intended to concentrate on capturing Zepa. There was a very close connection between those enclaves, both, for all sorts of reasons. Zepa enclave was, as I think you are aware of, very small but very rugged terrain and [indiscernible] a very difficult place also from the purely military point of view. I think there was a Ukrainian UN component there as well. Well, there was some difficulty associated with that. To make this long story short, Mr. Muratovic wanted my help to communicate with Mr. Milosevic on the possibility for the remaining HBiH [sic] units to evacuate Zepa to Serbia. This was somewhat surprising demand to me, but I said, I'm your humble servant, more or less. If you think it is better to bring them out of Serbia and you think that is safe, he said, We don't know, but can we get assurances from Milosevic that he would receive our fighters. Because the -- if you look at the map, Zepa is closer to Serbia than it is to Sarajevo territory and obviously -- fairly obviously, I would say, Bosnian Serbs forces were concentrated in the area between Zepa and Sarajevo, but between Zepa and Serbia significantly less on extremely rugged terrain. I said I do what I can and then went and saw President Milosevic at the fairly distant location, another one of these Tito hideouts or lodges. And said to him this had to be a matter of extreme secrecy and said this is the case, can you guarantee that your forces will accept these people coming in. And he promised that. And I returned -- I sent that message back. I can't really remember by which way but some secure way of communication to Prime Minister Muratovic and eventually this is what happened. They were later taken in by the UNHCR in a special camp in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Serbia. And there was some issues with them later after the war, because obviously Sarajevo wanted them [indiscernible] come back to Sarajevo, some of them did, but quite a number of them wanted to go elsewhere. And I think a fair number of them, as a matter of fact, settled in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Only one quick matter which is I believe on line 17. It should read -- page 61, line 17, it should read "evacuate the BiH to Serbia." Sorry? Army -- it should read "evacuate the Army of the BiH to Serbia."

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: The remaining fighters of the unit of the HBiH which was, of course, was the locals in Zepa to large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your labours are certainly not done yet in terms of what is occurring at this time. And I now would like to move on and focus on another issue, which is the issue of the French pilots who were shot down, if I might. First of all, do you recall when they were shot down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a subject matter that is not contained, Your Honour, in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon is correct in that respect, but to the extent that it plays upon the ultimate issue of Dayton and -- I think that it's relevant for the Chamber to have some understanding of what occurred. I certainly don't think that it is something that the Chamber should not be aware of. I appreciate what Mr. Harmon has said and to that extent I do apologise to Mr. Harmon. I wasn't trying to pull a fast one on him in any sense whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the ultimate issue of Dayton is in this proceeding, Your Honour, so I'm not sure it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my problem and I don't know too. And I -- I understand you were not trying to play a fast one on Mr. Harmon, but unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you've got to play the game also by the rules and the rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me explain to you -- let me explain to you precisely what I'm getting at which is that the French pilots were shot done. There were negotiations for the release of the French pilots. The issue of the release of the French pilots was something that President Chirac made a, as a term I used before, a condition precedent to the signing at the Paris peace conference on December 14th. And the question -- and that's the beginning an end of it [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Perhaps we must talk about the Paris conference on the 14th and find out from the witness how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, okay, fine. I'm just trying to -- trying to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In effect, it is more helpful if you do it the way I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- because then are you dealing with something that you have given notice about and you can tell us how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the French pilots are part of the step towards, so shall it be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let us move to the 14th of December, then, if we could. Do you recall what, if anything, occurred on the 14th of December that was of the moment?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: There was the signing -- if I remember, the signing of the Dayton agreement on peace, as it was called, for Bosnia and Herzegovina in Paris. I mean, what is referred to as the Dayton Agreement was initialed in Dayton on November the 21st, I don't remember really but something along those lines, and was signed formally in Paris on December the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to signing on the 14th, were there any conditions that existed prior to that document being signed and that agreement being entered into by the French government?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of but I know that you allude to the fact that they wanted to add the French -- there were some French pilots who had been shot down and were held in -- by the VRS and that was obviously a concern of President Chirac. I was aware of this through the media. I don't really remember very much but I had no role whatsoever in that particular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your recollection of this matter, if you could take a look at your book at page 167 and see whether or not that helps refresh your recollection --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Sorry, in which page?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: 167. Okay. I'm happy to read my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's an excellent book, sir.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yeah, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so we don't run into the same problem that we had before, could you read it so that the Chamber is also aware of what's being said.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Should I read the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not the whole book, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That might help. "We were rapidly approaching the formal peace conference in Paris. However, President Chirac had declared that it could not take place until two French pilots captured by the Bosnian Serbs when their aircraft was shot down over Pale on August the 30th had been released. There was no reason to doubt his determination to make the meeting in Paris conditional on the release of the pilots."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. "I had raised the matter with various representatives of Pale on numerous occasions during the autumn." I stand corrected my memory was wrong. "We knew, from the pictures taken, that both pilots had survived and been detained. Even though there were some who believed that they were no longer alive, all the information available to be indicated they were still in Pale. Krajisnik played ignorant but promised to take up the issue in Pale and keep us informed. Naturally he did no such thing. Milosevic also said he knew nothing but promised to send some of his special police platoons to Bosnia to look for them. Whether he was telling the truth, I don't know, but his reference to the ability of his special police to operate in Bosnia was interesting. Indeed, this had implications in other context." Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as with regard to issue of whether or not this signing of the agreement that ultimately became the Dayton Agreement was conditioned by President Chirac on the release of the French pilots?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes. President Chirac, rightly so, was very concerned with the release of his pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, I would like to thank you for your time. I would like to thank you for your candor, and most particularly, I would like to thank you for the efforts that you engaged in during this tumultuous period in the history of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bildt.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a few questions. You were asked on -- a question by Defence counsel, on the 20th of July, 1995, whether you had heard or you were getting information about the massacres. In fact, prior to the 20th of July, as early as the 14th of July, you had received information that the men in Potocari had been separated from the women and children and that the men had disappeared. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And in respect of an answer that you gave to Defence counsel, this is the answer that you gave Defence counsel on page 59, starting at line 14, you were asked a question about foreseeability. And your answer was: "The one who is very worried about what might happen in Srebrenica was the Russian foreign minister," and you named him, I don't have the name recorded, "and the reason for that, I think, was the fact that he had been Russian foreign minister for quite some time, so he -- so I -- he been involved Srebrenica since 1993 and was perhaps more aware that many of the emotions and tensions surrounding that particular issue." Can you expand on that, please, that answer?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, I could. Of course, when I'm saying this, I said the only one who brought it up with me. It doesn't necessarily mean the only one in the international community. But I said, I was dealing primarily with the political aspects but occasionally, of course, people said to me certain things concerning be aware of that and be aware of that, concerning developments on the ground. I remember Lord Owen handing over to him, asking me to keep a particular eye on a particular -- other spots. It wasn't this particular one. The one who really said to me keep an eye on this, on Srebrenica, was the Russian foreign minister. And my sort of theory for that, going back, I mean, this is not something -- I did note it and I took a note of it at the time. And then when I went back, of course, after the massacre and the genocide, of course, then you go back over this issue and said why was it him and no one else? Then it is my explanation to myself that that is the reason why it was him. Because he had been around for a long time and knew the issue quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What precisely was he worried about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, what precisely was the Russian foreign minister worried about in respect of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I can't remember how he phrased it. I went, saw him, this was in the very early stage of my mission when I went around and looked -- I mean, really, I started by seeing sort all of the main actors of the international drama and, of course, Russia, key country, US, UK, France, those were the key ones and then, of course, the UN, others. So I went down and see him, and I knew him quite well, since previous dealings on other issues. Went down and had dinner with him in Soci, by the Black Sea, and later on, I mean, when I was writing my book, when I went back over my notes I was struck by this particular fact that he had said something, beware of Srebrenica, and that's roughly what he said. I can't remember more than that. But it was a very emotional and sensitive issue obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was his concern about the enclave itself, was his concern about the people in the enclave? What was the focus, as you recall, what was the focus of his concern that he told you to be aware of?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: If I were to interpret it, but take it as it is, it was that he was aware of this being a very sensitive issue where emotions were running very high. Accordingly, where things could go extremely wrong from his -- from the humanitarian point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: There had been a lot of evil committed around it. And a lot of feelings of evil around Srebrenica. I wouldn't say this was the only place, needless to say. But he indicated to me at that particular time, and I do not -- and I said, this was something that I found in my own notes when I was writing my books, two years after the event, and it really struck me that he was the only one who pointed at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember -- are you able to remember the interpretation of this warning by him at the time it was made, that is, before Srebrenica took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this was -- yeah. We, of course, in those sorts of discussions you sort of mentioned -- which I had naturally with all of the foreign ministers, where were the sensitive points, where were the difficulties in achieving peace. It was mainly dealing with the political issues, sometimes we mentioned sort of certain areas. Needless to say, the main concern of the international community was on Sarajevo, but it was also on the enclaves. I would also say that a lot of concern was on the situation in the west, around the Krajinas; and later, of course, that exploded. Just after the eastern front exploded, which was just after the major fighting around Sarajevo during this rather horrible summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have an exhibit on the monitor, please. It is P1089.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, what you're going to be seeing and what I'm going to be directing your attention to is an article, and I'm going to direct your attention specifically to some comments by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadaka Ogata, and I'd like you to comment on that. You'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could get a little bit larger text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is not the article.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is not P1089. This is not the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an AFB telegram but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, this is not the document I've called up. Perhaps the wrong document has been uploaded into court. But this is ... we can use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you go down to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. I have no difficulty at all with you using the document obviously if it is on the list on one fashion or another, but I'd like to know what document I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, this should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- dealing with, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify that because it needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is P1089. This is the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt, if we could go down to the fifth paragraph, it starts with the words: "In Geneva ..." Can you read that? It says that in Geneva the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, called the wholesale removal from Srebrenica residents one of the most blatant examples of ethnically motivated forced displacement we have seen yet in the war. And this is dated on the 13th of July, 1995, when she made those remarks. Can you comment on -- first of all, were you aware of the forcible displacement of people from Srebrenica on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And that was -- I should not really comment too much on what the UN did and did not to. But, of course, there was an ethical dilemma involved in it from the UN side, in the sense that part of this was facilitated by the UN and that is why we had talked with President Izetbegovic because if we take the women and the men [indiscernible] what was taken out of Srebrenica courtesy of the UN. The men were then separated -- or some of the men were separated then we have the big column all together, of course. It was a complete cleansing of Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And was the cleansing of Srebrenica foreseeable assuming it was taken over by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think there was any -- any doubt on that, that if an enclave was taken -- I mean, that was unfortunately the pattern of a large part of the Bosnian war. When an army conquered the territory, consequences did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Amongst those consequences was murder?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One of the consequences?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: More or less. In this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In this case there was an extraordinary --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- murder on a larger scale --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- than what had been seen before. But was murder a foreseeable consequence of the takeover of the Srebrenica enclave? Not on the scale that we're talking about, that we now know historically took place.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I mean, difficult to say. In retrospect, of course. In retrospect, of course, but murder on this -- because what happened here was -- of course, particularly the fact that people who had been sort of -- the men who had been separated, who had been taken to different sort of encampments in schools and facilities, and you know this extremely well, that they were sort of massacred in large numbers. I mean, thousands after thousands after thousands. That had never happened before during the Bosnian war. Indeed, it is rather unique in post-war European history. It is unique in the post-war European history, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Putting aside the scale of the murders, in the Bosnian war historically when territory was taken over and ethnically cleansed, in part, part of that ethnic cleansing included the killing of the ethnic group that had been conquered?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Not necessarily entire ethnic group --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not the entire ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Individuals of the ethnic group, absolutely, if you go through the history of the Bosnian war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So when Srebrenica was taken over by the Bosnian Serb army, was it foreseeable that there would be killings with the conquest of that territory?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: It was foreseeable that there would be a -- connection with fighting or connection with remnants of fighting, or a connection with retribution, or connection with revenge, or connection with something else. Unfortunately, that was the nature of that war. But then, as said, now we're talking about what would unfortunately we call the normal picture of the war, but what subsequently happened in Srebrenica goes well beyond even the rather horrendous normal picture of horrendous war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So your answer to my question was: Yes, it was foreseeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think that was the answer to your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if it was an answer that was conditioned upon a series of factors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... was the genocide foreseeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about the genocide. I'm asking about the killings. Were the killings -- were killings --

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- foreseeable when the territory was ethnically cleansed.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Killings, yes. The killings is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, and that's why I put aside the question of the scale.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me discuss my last point, and that is, you discussed at the end of your evidence, you discussed Zepa, and you said there had been agreement with Mr. Milosevic that the -- that he would accept members of the ABiH who'd come over from Zepa. And let me just ask you this question, Mr. Bildt. Notwithstanding that agreement with Mr. Milosevic, to your knowledge, were some of the ABiH soldiers who had made it to Serbian territory, in fact, returned to the Republika Srpska, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Don't know. I know there were other killings in connection with Zepa. I mean, notably the commander, of course, in the -- who was -- I think you are aware of this particular incident, when they were in the final stages of the Zepa drama, there was a negotiation or talk between -- I don't know who it was, with the UN commander, and there was Mladic, and there was commander of the HBiH forces in Zepa, and there was the Ukrainian UN people. The Bosnian army commander was then taken away, and I think it had been confirmed that he was killed directly after those negotiations or talks. So, of course, there were also substantial killings in the times of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bildt. I have no additional questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is past time for the break. Do you have any questions for re-examination, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have about a minute and a half and I would be able to answer that question. I don't know if the Chamber has any questions. And I am appreciative also of Mr. Bildt's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Bildt's schedule. So if I could have but a second. Because if I have a question, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question is this. With regard to the issue of killings being foreseeable, you indicated that it was foreseeable that killings with the conquest of territory could occur for a number of reasons. Those reasons, as I understood your answer, included fighting between the warring factions, the remnants of the warring factions, retribution. And then you mentioned something else?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: I probably did. What? Revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Revenge, okay.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Probably. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying desperately to get you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have but two very short questions for you, sir. My first question is the following. When you met President Milosevic in Belgrade around the 14th and 15th of July, 1995, according to you, was he aware of the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Of course he was. I mean, the events of Srebrenica -- well, depends on -- now we have to define --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm talking about massacres, in fact.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: That I don't know. That I don't know. But clearly we were -- I mean, the fall of Srebrenica was on the 11th. Srebrenica was headlines all over the world by that particular time. It had fundamentally changed the diplomatic discourse. He was aware of the letter of warning I had sent him. He was aware of the intense diplomatic activity under way. I -- I -- immediately when I saw him, I said, Mr. Milosevic, you understand that this has changed everything. You are now in a different situation, and we are in a different situation, and you have to act accordingly. So he was clearly aware of -- I mean, the genocide comes later. Well, awareness of the genocide comes later, to be precise. But the fall of the -- Srebrenica in itself, the fall of an enclave, was such a serious event in itself and the humanitarian issues that we were aware of at the time were such a serious event in themselves that it changed the entire discourse. And that he was aware of. And we made him even more aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I was only talking about, in fact, the information that he may have had about massacres that may have taken -- that took in place in the enclave. If you don't know, then I got my answer. Now, my following question is the following. You said that the contact groups were refusing to have contacts with Karadzic and that the only contact, in order to stop the war or to try to negotiate, was -- was Milosevic. So my question is as follows. Was that sufficient for negotiators to convince Milosevic or to pressure Milosevic in order to stop the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: A very good question. History happens only once. That was the decisions that had been taken by the key capitals. And you can say that in retrospect, yes, the war was been stopped. I think the key question is, really, would it have been possible to close down the war earlier, and that's for the historians to debate. Clearly the summer of 1995 was exceedingly horrible, in terms of both massacre, genocide, ethnic cleansing, different sides. Clearly the worse since it's war in 1992. Would it have been possible for some sort of diplomatic initiative prior to that, I wasn't around the Bosnian scene at that particular time, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, in fact, my question was little bit more -- was focussing something else, in fact. During the entire trial, he was saying that Bosnian Serbs would not have been able to survive without the material help from Serbs from Serbia. So if the Serbs from Serbia had stopped to -- to help, in terms of giving the them the material -- material help, would that have stopped the war?

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Well, that is, of course, what we tried to do. There had been the Drina blockade since I can't remember exactly when. But prior to me entering the scene, Milosevic had agreed to impose a complete embargo on Republika Srpska, and as -- I had a co-responsibility from the ICFY for the ICFY border monitoring mission, I think the name of it was. We had monitors along the Drina to try to see if there were any major supplies coming through. And I spent quite some time, and I had a special American team under me trying to see if there were any signs of major resupply of Bosnian Serb forces from Serbia. So we were clearly -- and there's no doubt that there was smuggling. But whether there was any major resupply, we did not, with the monitors that we had in place on all of the crossing points and all of the bridges, detect any major smuggling. Could there have been? With helicopters and hidden pipe-lines and the small supplies, I'm quite certain there was. But we spent quite some time trying to find out, for example, how the Bosnian Serbs forces were supplied with fuel, which is an interesting question. But when you went into that interesting question, you also found that there were many dimensions to the war in Bosnia, and there were very many who were prepared to trade in ways that you would not necessarily think of immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quickly, quickly, are there any questions arising from the questions by the Judge? Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the very end of your answer, sir, to Judge Picard's question, which is when you went into that interesting question you found that there were many, many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Dimensions. Thank you. The language of the question, as it is written here, is a bit funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you expand, please, on what you mean by that: Many, many dimensions.

utterances.speaker: CARL BILDT
utterances.text: Every war produces, and every sanctions produces black markets. There are always people who are prepared to make money independent of ethnicity and political loyalties in the middle of a war. And in this particular war, there was no difference. So as far as weapons were concerned, there was no need for that, because there was an abundance of weapons in the area that had to do with the fact that, of course, Bosnia was the most heavily militarised part of former Yugoslavia, because that is where the Yugoslav Army had prepared these last bastions in defence against an invasion. So there was both territorial army, and VJ, and arms depots, and arms factories, and enormous amounts of both arms and ammunition in enormous quantities. I mean, military -- western military people who came there subsequently looked at the ammunition dumps were really surprised by the magnitude of how the Yugoslavs had stored ammunition for a prolonged war. That had to do the wartime history of Tito and the partisans. Fuel you could buy on the black markets. Then there was also a lot of smuggling of beer and cigarettes, because it turned out that on Republika Srpska territory there was no brewery. And there was no cigarette factory. The cigarette factory was in Sarajevo, and the breweries were elsewhere. Soldiers want beer and they want cigarettes. So that was also commodities that were very high demand and were smuggled in not in significant quantities across the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

Please travel well back home. I hope you can still make your appointment in Stockholm.
